config.title: Mould in a Berlin Flat - FAQ
config.subtitle: When airing actually dries a Berlin room and when it wets it, the hour to open the window in summer, the wall temperature where mould starts, what tight new windows changed in an old building, and what a landlord can and cannot demand.

items.q: Does opening the window really dry out a Berlin flat?
items.a: It depends entirely on the month. Outdoor air only takes water away if it carries less than the air inside. A living room at 20 °C and 60 percent humidity holds 10.4 grams of water per cubic metre. Averaged over ten complete years at the Deutscher Wetterdienst station in Berlin-Tempelhof, Berlin outdoor air holds 4.9 g/m³ in January, 8.3 in October, 9.6 in September and 11.1 in August. So a five minute airing in January strips 5.5 grams from every cubic metre it swaps, while the same airing in August puts about 0.7 grams in. Across the whole grid of twelve months by twenty four hours, 49 of the 288 hours make that room wetter and another 68 move less than half a gram.

items.q: What time of day should I air my flat in Berlin?
items.a: In summer, mid afternoon. The instinct to open up early because the air feels cool and fresh is wrong from June to August in Berlin. Moisture collects near the ground overnight and drier air mixes down through the day, so the dew point falls while the thermometer climbs. In July the air at 06:00 carries 11.3 grams per cubic metre and at 16:00 only 10.2. In August it is 11.6 at 07:00 against 10.4 at 15:00. From November to March the hour hardly matters: the whole of January sits inside a 0.2 gram band, so air whenever it suits you.

items.q: How cold does a wall have to be before mould grows on it?
items.a: Colder than you would guess from looking for water. The Umweltbundesamt's mould guide puts the growth threshold at 70 to 80 percent relative humidity at the surface of the material, sustained over time, and says explicitly that materials do not have to be visibly wet. In a room at 20 °C and 60 percent humidity, any surface below 15.4 °C sits at that 80 percent line, while droplets only appear below 12.0 °C. That leaves about 3.4 degrees in which mould has what it needs and you get no visual warning. The usual Berlin candidates are the window reveal, the outer corner of a rear-building room, and the wall behind a wardrobe pushed flat against the outside masonry.

items.q: Why did my Berlin flat get damp after the landlord fitted new windows?
items.a: Because the old windows were ventilating the flat for you. The Umweltbundesamt models exactly this case: an untouched old flat has an infiltration rate around 0.5 air changes per hour, which is twelve complete air changes a day that nobody has to remember, and its model bedroom stays clear on a single morning airing even with laundry drying in the room. Fit tight modern windows and leave the walls uninsulated, which is the most common retrofit in Berlin, and infiltration falls to roughly 0.1 per hour, about 2.4 free changes a day. The guide's own conclusion is that the airing frequency then required is barely achieved in practice.

items.q: How much water does a household put into the air each day?
items.a: The Umweltbundesamt gives 6 to 12 litres a day for an average three-person household. The components it lists are 30 to 40 grams an hour per person at light activity, about a quarter of a litre per person per night in a bedroom, and 50 to 200 grams an hour from a 4.5 kilogram drum of spun laundry, rising to 100 to 500 grams an hour if it is dripping wet. For comparison, one complete air change of a 70 square metre Berlin flat with three metre ceilings removes about 1.15 litres in January and adds about 0.15 litres in August.

items.q: Can I reduce my rent in Berlin because of mould?
items.a: Not simply because the outside walls are cold. On 5 December 2018 the Bundesgerichtshof decided VIII ZR 271/17 and VIII ZR 67/18 on two buildings from 1968 and 1971, overturning a 20 percent rent reduction and holding that thermal bridges in the outer walls are not a defect when the building matches the building codes and technical standards in force when it was built. Almost every Berlin Altbau meets the standards of its own construction date by definition. The same case is more helpful on what can be asked of you: the lower court held that airing twice a day for up to ten minutes was the fair limit, and that a tenant cannot be required to keep bedrooms below 16 °C or other rooms below 20 °C, while the court expert calculated that twice daily for about 15 minutes, or three times daily for about 10 minutes, would have prevented the mould. Take a dated photo log and hygrometer readings to the Berliner Mieterverein or another tenants' association before deducting anything.

No, and in the cold months it can cause the problem it is meant to solve. The Umweltbundesamt calls wide open and cross ventilation the means of choice and says tilt airing is markedly less effective and would have to run far longer. It also warns that long spells on the tilt setting strongly cool the window reveal and the lintel, and that condensation then forms on those cooled surfaces, which is exactly where mould appears in a Berlin flat. It also wastes a great deal of heating energy. Open two windows on opposite sides of the flat fully, for five minutes, then shut everything.

items.q: What should I do about damp in a Berlin flat this autumn?
items.a: Until about mid October the window is doing under a gram per cubic metre, so work on the sources: lid on the pan, extractor on, wet laundry out of the flat, bathroom door shut with the window open while the shower is still steaming. From mid October the numbers pass two grams and climb, so build the habit of wide open cross airing for five minutes, twice a day, plus once more after a shower or a big cook. Put a ten euro hygrometer in the coldest room rather than the living room, and pull solid furniture 5 to 10 cm off the outside walls. Keep bedrooms between 16 and 18 °C with the door to the warm rooms closed.
